patient.name: Kofi Asante
patient.complaint: Severe headache, fever and vomiting for 12 hours, now drowsy
background: First-year student at King's, living in halls for 3 weeks
Missed his MenACWY vaccine at school
Shares a kitchen with six flatmates

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'Which is the most likely causative organism?' with fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. Age, rash, CSF Gram stain and risk factors (otitis, soft cheese, HIV) name the organism.

points: 12 hours of **severe headache**, fever and vomiting.
Light hurts his eyes; neck feels stiff.
His flatmate says he is getting drowsy.

steps.lead: Kofi's fever with headache and neck stiffness is **meningeal irritation**: the meninges are inflamed.

points: Neck flexion is painful and resisted.
Lifting his head makes his hips and knees flex.
Extending his knee with the hip flexed hurts his back.
Glass test on his skin: **no rash**.

steps.lead: Kofi has the classic symptoms plus positive **Brudzinski's** (neck flexion bends the hips) and **Kernig's** signs.

steps.q: An 18 year old fresher in halls with bacterial meningitis. Which organism is most likely?
steps.r: **N. meningitidis** peaks at 5 months and again at **adolescence/university entry**. Pneumococcus is the commonest in older adults.

steps.lead: Kofi is severely ill and deteriorating fast: **bacterial**, most likely meningococcal at his age. Viral meningitis is milder and self-limiting.
Kofi is not immunocompromised. A patient with HIV and a subacute headache would make you think of **cryptococcal** meningitis.
Kofi's GCS is 14 with no focal signs, seizures or papilloedema, and no rash: **no contraindication** to LP and no need for CT first.

steps.title: Can Kofi have an LP now?
nodes: Septicaemia or rapidly evolving rash? → no LP
GCS <13, focal deficit, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromise? → CT head first
None present → LP (ideally before antibiotics, within 1 hour)

steps.lead: Kofi's biggest long-term risk is **sensorineural hearing loss**, so he will need a hearing test after recovery.

steps.text: No rash does **not** exclude meningococcal disease. Many patients never develop one; a non-blanching rash means **septicaemia**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (LP, or CT head first if raised ICP signs), and CSF tables where you must say bacterial, viral or cryptococcal.

steps.q: Kofi has no contraindications. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: **LP** is the diagnostic first-line test. Blood cultures are taken too, but CSF confirms meningitis.

steps.lead: Kofi's **LP** is done within the hour with blood cultures. If he had septicaemia, **whole blood PCR** would identify the organism instead.

steps.title: Kofi's CSF
steps.text: Turbid, neutrophils, high protein, glucose less than half of serum: bacterial. Gram-negative diplococci: meningococcus.

visual.title: CSF : serum glucose ratio
visual.label: Kofi 0.25
visual.caption: Bacteria consume glucose; viruses do not.

steps.lead: Kofi's CSF is the **bacterial** pattern. Viral would be clear with lymphocytes; cryptococcal needs an **India ink** stain.

visual.title: Kofi's GCS on the ward
visual.caption: A drop to 12 at 4 hours triggers immediate ICU referral.

steps.lead: When Kofi's GCS drops to 12, he needs **immediate ICU referral** for escalating care.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IM benzylpenicillin in primary care, IV ceftriaxone in A&E (add amoxicillin for Listeria if very young, over 60 or pregnant), dexamethasone within 4 hours unless septicaemia, and ciprofloxacin for close contacts.

steps.q: Kofi was first seen by his GP, who suspected meningitis. What should the GP give before transfer?
steps.r: Primary care first line is **IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g** before urgent hospital transfer.

steps.lead: In ED Kofi, aged 18, gets **IV ceftriaxone**, switched to IV benzylpenicillin once the meningococcus proves sensitive.

steps.title: Empirical antibiotics by patient
nodes: A&E, over 3 months and under 60: IV ceftriaxone
Under 3 months, over 60, pregnant: add amoxicillin (Listeria)

steps.lead: Kofi has **no septicaemia**, so he gets **IV dexamethasone** with his first antibiotic dose.

visual.title: Dexamethasone window
visual.label: Kofi 30 min
visual.caption: Within 4 hours of IV antibiotics; not in meningococcal septicaemia.

steps.lead: Kofi's CSF is clearly bacterial. A patient with a viral picture would get **symptomatic care**, with aciclovir only if encephalitis were suspected.
Kofi's six flatmates are **close contacts** in the last 7 days: each gets a **single dose of oral ciprofloxacin**.
Kofi's care follows **NICE** meningitis guidance, and the UK public health team is notified to organise his contacts' prophylaxis.

steps.text: Do **not** delay antibiotics for a CT or LP. If the LP cannot happen within 1 hour, take blood cultures and give **ceftriaxone** now.
**Listeria** is not covered by ceftriaxone. Under 3 months, over 60, pregnant or immunocompromised: add **amoxicillin**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the rash forms, why dexamethasone helps, why CSF glucose is low in bacterial and normal in viral meningitis.

steps.lead: Kofi's turbid, neutrophil-rich CSF and raised pressure come from an intense **inflammatory response** in the subarachnoid space.
Kofi had no rash, but if meningococcal **endotoxin** reaches the blood it drives **DIC** and a non-blanching purpuric rash.

steps.q: Why was dexamethasone given with Kofi's first antibiotic dose?
o: It limits inflammation from bacterial lysis
steps.r: Antibiotics lyse bacteria, releasing a burst of inflammatory products. **Dexamethasone** damps this, limiting neurological damage and **hearing loss**.

steps.lead: Kofi's dexamethasone limits the inflammation that his antibiotics trigger, protecting his **hearing**.
Kofi's CSF glucose is low because bacteria **consume** it. In viral meningitis it stays normal and there is no purulent response.

visual.title: Kofi's recovery
visual.caption: CRP peaks on day 1 then falls on benzylpenicillin. Hearing test before discharge.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in the UK?
mcq.r: **N. meningitidis** (Gram-negative diplococci); pneumococcus is commonest in adults.

mcq.q: What is the most common complication of meningitis?
Which organism is a Gram-positive rod linked to soft cheese and pregnancy?
Which is a contraindication to lumbar puncture in meningitis?
mcq.r: **Septicaemia** and raised ICP (GCS <13, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema) contraindicate LP.

mcq.q: Which CSF result fits bacterial meningitis?
mcq.r: **Neutrophils, high protein, glucose below half serum**, turbid, raised opening pressure.

mcq.q: Which stain is diagnostic for cryptococcal meningitis?
What is given in primary care for suspected meningitis?
When is dexamethasone contraindicated in meningitis?
mcq.r: Contraindicated in **suspected meningococcal septicaemia**; give within 4 hours of antibiotics otherwise.

mcq.q: What prophylaxis do close meningococcal contacts receive?
mcq.r: **Single-dose oral ciprofloxacin**; rifampicin is the alternative.

mcq.q: What causes the meningococcal non-blanching rash?

technique.stem: A 19 year old woman in university halls has a 10 hour history of severe headache, vomiting and fever. She is drowsy and cannot tolerate light. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. She has neck stiffness and a non-blanching petechial rash on her legs.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of headache with fever: infection or bleed?
Rapid, severe febrile illness with meningism and a **non-blanching rash** in a student.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis** with septicaemia.

elim: Migraine does not cause fever, meningism and a rash.
SAH is a sudden thunderclap headache without fever or rash.
Tension headache is a band-like pain with no systemic illness.
Viral meningitis is milder and does not cause a petechial rash or shock.

steps.x: **A. Bacterial meningitis.** Rule: fever + meningism + non-blanching rash = meningococcal; treat immediately.

technique.stem: A 27 year old man has a 1 day history of headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. His GCS is 15. There is no rash, no focal neurology and no papilloedema. He is not immunocompromised. Blood cultures have been taken.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' investigation for suspected meningitis.

clues: no rash, no focal neurology and no papilloedema
steps.x: No signs of raised ICP and no septicaemia: **no contraindication to LP**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lumbar puncture**, the diagnostic first-line test.

elim: Cultures are already taken; CSF is diagnostic.
CT is only needed first with raised ICP signs.
MRI does not diagnose meningitis.
Whole blood PCR is for when LP cannot be done.

steps.x: **C. Lumbar puncture.** Rule: no contraindication = LP; raised ICP signs = CT first.

technique.stem: A 32 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and confusion. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. There is no rash. He is not pregnant or immunocompromised and has no allergies. Blood cultures have been taken.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic?

steps.x: Initial antibiotic: check age, pregnancy and immune status.
Adult under 60, no Listeria risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV ceftriaxone** (with dexamethasone, as there is no septicaemia).

elim: Aciclovir is added only if encephalitis is suspected; it does not treat bacteria.
Amoxicillin is added for Listeria risk groups only.
Vancomycin is added for resistant pneumococcus after travel.
Ciprofloxacin is prophylaxis for contacts.

steps.x: **B. IV ceftriaxone.** Rule: 3 months to 60 years = ceftriaxone; outside that or pregnant, add amoxicillin.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man with pneumococcal meningitis is given IV dexamethasone 15 minutes before his first dose of IV ceftriaxone. A student asks why the steroid is given at this time.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which dexamethasone improves outcome?
o: Prevents bacterial adhesion to the meninges
Reduces inflammation from bacterial lysis after antibiotics

steps.x: Mechanism of an adjunct steroid.
The timing is the clue: it is given **with** the antibiotic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antibiotics lyse bacteria; dexamethasone **damps the inflammatory burst**, limiting neurological damage and hearing loss.

elim: Steroids are not antibacterial.
Steroids if anything reduce penetration by sealing the barrier.
It does not prevent adhesion.
It does not treat DIC; it is contraindicated in septicaemia.

steps.x: **D. Reduces inflammation from bacterial lysis.** Rule: give within 4 hours of antibiotics, not in septicaemia.

practice.stem: An 18 year old woman who started university 2 weeks ago has a 12 hour history of fever, headache and vomiting. Her temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. She has neck stiffness, photophobia and a non-blanching petechial rash on her trunk.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: A university entrant with meningitis and a non-blanching petechial rash has meningococcal disease. N. meningitidis peaks in infancy and again at adolescence/university entry.

steps.x: Causative organism: use age and rash.
University entry + bacterial meningitis + **petechial rash**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **N. meningitidis**.

elim: Viral meningitis is mild with no rash.
Rare since Hib vaccination.
Listeria affects neonates, over 60s, pregnant and immunocompromised.
Pneumococcus is older adults after otitis or pneumonia; no rash.

steps.x: **D. Neisseria meningitidis.** Rule: student + rash = meningococcus.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had a painful discharging left ear a week ago. He now has fever, severe headache and neck stiffness. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. There is no rash. Investigations (CSF):
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Gram-positive diplococci after otitis media in an adult is Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common cause in adults.

steps.x: Organism: the Gram stain decides.
Adult, after an **ear infection**; CSF bacterial with **Gram-positive diplococci**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **S. pneumoniae**.

elim: CSF is bacterial, not viral.
H. influenzae is Gram-negative coccobacilli.
Listeria is a Gram-positive rod.
Meningococcus is Gram-negative diplococci.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pneumoniae.** Rule: Gram-positive diplococci + otitis = pneumococcus.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 2 day history of headache, photophobia and mild neck stiffness after a sore throat last week. She is alert and orientated. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. There is no rash. Investigations (CSF):
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Mild meningism with normal mental state, clear CSF, lymphocytes, mildly raised protein and normal glucose after an upper respiratory illness is viral (usually enteroviral) meningitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: read the CSF.

clues: after a sore throat last week
steps.x: Mild illness, normal mental state; CSF clear, **lymphocytes**, normal glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Viral meningitis.**

elim: Bacterial gives neutrophils and low glucose.
Cryptococcal is in immunocompromised patients with low glucose.
Encephalitis causes confusion and seizures; she is alert.
SAH is sudden, with xanthochromia.

steps.x: **E. Viral meningitis.** Rule: lymphocytes + normal glucose + alert = viral.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant has fever, headache and neck stiffness. She has been eating unpasteurised soft cheese. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Investigations (CSF):
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Pregnancy, unpasteurised soft cheese and Gram-positive rods point to Listeria monocytogenes, which needs amoxicillin cover.

steps.x: Organism: risk group plus Gram stain.
Pregnancy and soft cheese; Gram stain shows **Gram-positive rods**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Listeria monocytogenes.**

elim: CSF is bacterial.
Gram-negative coccobacilli.
Gram-negative diplococci.
Gram-positive diplococci.

steps.x: **C. Listeria monocytogenes.** Rule: pregnant/over 60/neonate + Gram-positive rods = Listeria.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man with untreated HIV has a 3 week history of worsening headache, vomiting and fatigue. Today he had a seizure and is drowsy. He has mild neck stiffness. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Subacute headache, vomiting and fatigue progressing to seizures and drowsiness in advanced HIV, with raised protein and low glucose, is cryptococcal meningitis; India ink confirms it.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an immunocompromised patient.
Advanced HIV (CD4 45), **subacute** headache progressing to seizures; CSF high protein, low glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cryptococcal meningitis**: India ink stain.

elim: Bacterial is acute over hours, not 3 weeks.
Toxoplasmosis gives ring-enhancing masses and focal signs.
Lymphoma gives a focal mass lesion, not a meningitic CSF picture.
Viral has normal glucose and is mild.

steps.x: **C. Cryptococcal meningitis.** Rule: HIV + subacute headache + raised pressure = cryptococcus.

practice.stem: A 4 year old boy recovered from pneumococcal meningitis 2 months ago. His nursery reports he no longer responds when called from behind. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes and tympanometry is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
practice.e: Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common complication of meningitis. Normal drums and tympanometry exclude a conductive cause.

steps.x: A complication: what is the commonest after meningitis?
Hearing problem after meningitis with a normal middle ear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sensorineural hearing loss** (cochlear damage).

elim: Normal drums and tympanometry exclude conductive loss.
He responds to sight; the problem is sound.
Hydrocephalus would cause headache, vomiting or drowsiness.
An empyema causes fever and focal signs.

steps.x: **D. Sensorineural hearing loss.** Rule: every survivor needs a hearing test.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man has a 1 day history of fever, headache and neck stiffness. He had a generalised seizure in the ambulance. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg. His GCS is 11. Blood cultures have been taken and IV ceftriaxone given.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before lumbar puncture?
practice.e: A GCS below 13 and a new seizure are signs of possible raised ICP, so a CT head is needed before LP.

steps.x: What must be done **before** LP?
GCS <13 and a **new seizure**: raised ICP signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT head first.**

elim: Cultures are already taken.
EEG does not assess LP safety.
MRI spine is irrelevant.
Useful if LP is impossible, not a safety check.

steps.x: **B. CT head.** Rule: GCS <13, focal deficit, seizures, papilloedema or immunocompromise = CT before LP.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has fever, vomiting and a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. His temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 138 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and capillary refill time 5 seconds. IV ceftriaxone has been given. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the organism?
practice.e: Meningococcal septicaemia with a rapidly evolving rash and coagulopathy contraindicates LP, so whole blood PCR and blood cultures identify N. meningitidis.

steps.x: Identify the organism, without endangering him.
**Meningococcal septicaemia** with shock and DIC (low platelets, high INR): LP is contraindicated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Whole blood PCR** (plus blood cultures).

elim: Needs an LP, which is contraindicated.
CT does not identify the organism.
Throat swabs show carriage, not the cause.
Urine antigen is for pneumococcus or Legionella in pneumonia.

steps.x: **E. Whole blood PCR.** Rule: septicaemia = no LP; blood PCR instead.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man sees his GP with a 6 hour history of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. An ambulance has been called. He has no allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management before transfer?
practice.e: In primary care, suspected meningitis is treated with IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g before urgent hospital transfer.

steps.x: Primary care, before transfer.
Suspected bacterial meningitis in general practice.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g.**

elim: This is an emergency, not outpatient care.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate.
Ciprofloxacin is contact prophylaxis.
Delay could be fatal.

steps.x: **B. IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g.** Rule: GP = IM benzylpenicillin; A&E = IV ceftriaxone.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg. There is no rash. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic treatment?
practice.e: Over 60, Listeria must be covered: a third-generation cephalosporin plus IV amoxicillin.

steps.x: Initial antibiotics: check the age.
**Over 60**: Listeria risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cephalosporin + amoxicillin.**

elim: Does not treat bacteria.
Misses Listeria.
Gentamicin alone is inadequate.
Oral treatment is inadequate.

steps.x: **C. IV cefotaxime and IV amoxicillin.** Rule: over 60, under 3 months or pregnant = add amoxicillin.

practice.stem: A 19 year old student is admitted with confirmed meningococcal meningitis. His flatmate, who shares a kitchen with him and was with him 3 days ago, asks what she should do. She is well. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line management for the flatmate?
practice.e: Close contacts in the past 7 days receive a single dose of oral ciprofloxacin first line; rifampicin is the alternative.

steps.x: First-line **prophylaxis** for a well contact.
Close contact within **7 days**, no symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Single-dose oral ciprofloxacin.**

elim: Treatment for suspected disease, not prophylaxis.
Vaccination alone does not clear carriage now.
She is a close contact and needs prophylaxis.
Rifampicin is the alternative, not first line.

steps.x: **D. Oral ciprofloxacin single dose.** Rule: close contact within 7 days = ciprofloxacin.

practice.stem: A 16 year old girl has meningococcal septicaemia with a spreading purpuric rash. Her platelet count is low, INR is prolonged and fibrinogen is low.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her rash?
practice.e: Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide endotoxin drives DIC, consuming platelets and clotting factors and causing the non-blanching purpuric rash.

steps.x: Mechanism of the rash.
Consumption of platelets **and** clotting factors: **DIC**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) → DIC → purpura.**

elim: Immune complex vasculitis is e.g. HSP; fibrinogen would be normal.
ITP does not prolong the INR or lower fibrinogen.
Marrow suppression does not lower fibrinogen.
Vitamin K deficiency spares platelets and fibrinogen.

steps.x: **A. Endotoxin-driven DIC.** Rule: low platelets + high INR + low fibrinogen = DIC.

prompts.q: What is meningitis and what are its symptoms and signs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever plus meningism; then decide viral or bacterial.

points.p: Inflammation of the meninges, bacterial or viral
Headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea
points.why: Not all are present in every patient.

points.p: Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs

prompts.q: Which bacteria cause meningitis, in whom, and what does the Gram stain show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age, risk factor and Gram stain name the organism.

points.p: N. meningitidis: Gram-negative diplococci; infants and teenagers/university; petechial rash
S. pneumoniae: Gram-positive diplococci; adults, after otitis or pneumonia
Listeria: Gram-positive rod; neonates, elderly, pregnant, immunocompromised
Group B Strep: most common in neonates; also E. coli, H. influenzae
points.why: Hence cefotaxime and ampicillin in infants.

prompts.q: How does viral meningitis differ from bacterial, and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mild, alert, after a summer flu.

points.p: Enteroviruses most common (echo, coxsackie, polio), hand-to-mouth
Milder, self-limiting, good prognosis
points.why: Bacterial is severe, rapid and an emergency.

points.p: May follow an upper respiratory illness

prompts.q: What are the complications of meningitis, and which special type affects people with HIV?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hearing test after recovery.

points.p: Most common: sensorineural hearing loss
Brain damage, seizures, death
points.why: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency.

points.p: Cryptococcal meningitis in immunocompromised (HIV)
points.why: Subacute headache, vomiting, fatigue, then seizures.

prompts.q: When is lumbar puncture contraindicated, and what do you do instead?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: list the raised ICP signs.

points.p: Meningococcal septicaemia
points.why: Also rapidly evolving rash or bleeding risk.

points.p: Raised ICP: GCS <13, focal deficit, new seizures, papilloedema
points.why: Also immunocompromise, known CNS lesion, postural headache.

points.p: CT head first in these cases
points.why: Never delay antibiotics for the CT.

prompts.q: What is the diagnostic test, and what if it cannot be done?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: LP within 1 hour, ideally before antibiotics.

points.p: Lumbar puncture: diagnostic first line
points.why: Ideally before antibiotics if within 1 hour.

points.p: If LP impossible: whole blood PCR and blood cultures
Drop in GCS: immediate ICU referral

prompts.q: Compare CSF in bacterial, viral and cryptococcal meningitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cells and glucose decide.

points.p: Bacterial: turbid, neutrophils, high protein, glucose under half serum, high pressure
Viral: clear, lymphocytes, protein 0.5 to 1 g/L, normal glucose
Cryptococcal: raised protein, low glucose, India ink diagnostic

prompts.q: Which antibiotics are given, by setting and patient group?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: GP vs A&E, then age and pregnancy.

points.p: GP: IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g before transfer
A&E, 3 months to 60 years: IV ceftriaxone
points.why: Switch to benzylpenicillin if sensitive meningococcus.

points.p: Under 3 months, over 60, pregnant: add amoxicillin for Listeria
Add vancomycin for resistant pneumococcus; chloramphenicol if allergic
Add IV aciclovir if encephalitis suspected

prompts.q: When is dexamethasone given, and what do close contacts receive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: septicaemia rules out steroids.

points.p: IV dexamethasone within 4 hours of IV antibiotics
points.why: Reduces morbidity, mortality and hearing loss.

points.p: Contraindicated in meningococcal septicaemia
Contacts within 7 days: single dose oral ciprofloxacin (or rifampicin)

prompts.q: What happens in bacterial meningitis, why the rash, and why is CSF glucose normal in viral?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: inflammation, endotoxin, glucose consumption.

points.p: Neutrophil influx, cytokines, blood-brain barrier breakdown, cerebral oedema, raised ICP
Meningococcal endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) drives DIC and purpura
points.why: Low platelets, high INR, low fibrinogen.

points.p: Dexamethasone limits inflammation from antibiotic-induced bacterial lysis
Viral: no purulent response; glucose not consumed

glossary.Meningitis: Inflammation of the meninges, the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Meninges: The three membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from irritated meninges.
glossary.Kernig's sign: Pain and resistance when extending the knee with the hip flexed.
glossary.Brudzinski's sign: Passive neck flexion causes the hips and knees to flex.
glossary.Petechial: Tiny pinpoint bleeding spots in the skin that do not blanch.
glossary.Purpuric: Larger non-blanching purple patches from bleeding into the skin.
glossary.Glass test: Pressing a glass on a rash; if it stays visible it is non-blanching.
glossary.Septicaemia: Bacteria multiplying in the blood with a systemic response.
glossary.N. meningitidis: Neisseria meningitidis, a Gram-negative diplococcus and the commonest UK cause of bacterial meningitis.
glossary.Neisseria meningitidis: The meningococcus, a Gram-negative diplococcus causing meningitis and septicaemia.
glossary.S. pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram-positive diplococcus and the commonest adult cause.
glossary.Streptococcus pneumoniae: The pneumococcus, a Gram-positive diplococcus causing meningitis after otitis or pneumonia.
glossary.Listeria: A Gram-positive rod infecting neonates, over 60s, pregnant and immunocompromised people.
glossary.Listeria monocytogenes: A Gram-positive rod spread by soft cheese and unpasteurised milk.
glossary.Group B Streptococcus: The commonest cause of neonatal meningitis, passed from mother at birth.
glossary.Enteroviruses: Viruses such as coxsackie and echovirus, the commonest cause of viral meningitis.
glossary.Diplococci: Bacteria seen in pairs of round cells on microscopy.
glossary.Cryptococcal meningitis: Fungal meningitis in immunocompromised people such as those with advanced HIV.
glossary.India ink: A stain that outlines the capsule of Cryptococcus in CSF.
glossary.CD4: A type of T helper cell; a low count shows advanced HIV.
glossary.Lumbar puncture: A needle into the lower spine to sample cerebrospinal fluid.
glossary.CSF: Cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Opening pressure: CSF pressure measured at the start of an LP; raised in bacterial meningitis.
glossary.Turbid: Cloudy, as CSF looks when full of white cells.
glossary.Polymorphonuclear: Neutrophils; the white cells that dominate CSF in bacterial meningitis.
glossary.Xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from broken-down blood, typical of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
glossary.Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic disc from raised intracranial pressure.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, scored 3 to 15; below 13 means CT before LP.
glossary.Whole blood PCR: A blood test that detects meningococcal DNA when LP cannot be done.
glossary.Benzylpenicillin: Penicillin G; given IM by the GP for suspected meningitis.
glossary.Ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin, first-line IV treatment for bacterial meningitis in A&E.
glossary.Cefotaxime: A third-generation cephalosporin used in infants and with amoxicillin in Listeria risk groups.
glossary.Chloramphenicol: An alternative antibiotic when penicillins and cephalosporins cannot be used.
glossary.Vancomycin: Added when resistant pneumococcus is possible, such as after travel.
glossary.Dexamethasone: A steroid given within 4 hours of antibiotics to reduce neurological damage and hearing loss.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic given as a single oral dose to close contacts.
glossary.Rifampicin: An alternative prophylactic antibiotic for meningococcal contacts.
glossary.Prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent disease in someone exposed.
glossary.Endotoxin: A toxic component of the outer wall of Gram-negative bacteria.
glossary.Lipooligosaccharide: The meningococcal endotoxin that triggers DIC and shock.
glossary.DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting factors.
glossary.Sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing loss from inner ear or nerve damage; the commonest complication of meningitis.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: The tight lining of brain capillaries that controls what enters the brain.
glossary.Cerebral oedema: Swelling of the brain that raises intracranial pressure.
glossary.MenACWY: A vaccine against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y, offered to teenagers.
